nodes.p: Receives files and whole folders the person drags onto the page, with no prompt.
nodes.m: Dropping is consent for exactly what is dropped, including folder trees. The site can read file contents and, in Chrome, ask for write access to the dropped items.
nodes.api: drop event; dataTransfer.files; items; webkitGetAsEntry(); getAsFileSystemHandle()
nodes.ps: Per drop
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Opens the system file chooser; the page gets only the files the person picks.
nodes.m: The most common way a site reaches a person's files. The person picks exactly what is shared, and the site sees name, size, type and modified time, but not the folder path.
nodes.api: <input type=file multiple accept=...>; input.files; File, FileList
nodes.ui: System file chooser dialog (the person picks files)
nodes.ps: Per selection; File objects live until the page unloads
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.n: File metadata (name, size, type, modified time)
nodes.p: Shows name, byte size, MIME type and last modified time of any file the person shares.
nodes.m: Metadata alone can reveal a lot: camera model names, document names, dates of work. The MIME type comes from the person's OS file associations, which also differs between machines.
nodes.api: File.name, size, type, lastModified, webkitRelativePath; Blob.slice(), arrayBuffer()
nodes.ps: While the File object lives
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.n: File System Access: open and save pickers
nodes.p: Lets the person pick files and then read and write them in place; Chromium only.
nodes.m: A site can open a local document, edit it and save over the original, like a desktop app. The person picks the file, and the browser asks again before write access.
nodes.ui: Chrome file chooser, then Edit files / Save changes permission bubble
nodes.ps: Handles can be stored in IndexedDB; Chrome 122 offers Allow on every visit persistent permission
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Gives the page a private, fast file system inside the browser, with no prompt.
nodes.m: A site can store large files and databases on disk invisibly to the person. It is sandboxed per site, but it can fill gigabytes of disk and survives until site data is cleared.
nodes.api: await navigator.storage.getDirectory(); createSyncAccessHandle() in a worker
nodes.ps: Persists until site data is cleared; best effort eviction until persist() is granted
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: The browser freezes a left page whole and restores it instantly on Back, with scripts and state intact.
nodes.m: A person who leaves and presses Back can resume the same JavaScript heap, form values and open connections. Analytics must treat pageshow with persisted=true as a new view. The page can run no code while frozen.
nodes.ps: Chrome keeps pages about 10 minutes (up to 6 entries on Android is not documented, verify)
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: Lets tabs and frames of the same site send messages to each other instantly.
nodes.m: A site can see that the same person has several tabs open and sync a login, logout or shopping state. Since partitioning, a tracker embed can no longer message its own copy on a different top site.
nodes.ps: While at least one context is open
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A store of HTTP responses used by service workers to serve pages offline.
nodes.m: Lets a site keep its own pages, scripts and API responses on the device. Shares the origin quota with IndexedDB. Opaque cross-origin responses are padded in quota accounting so sites cannot probe sizes.
nodes.ps: Until cleared or evicted. Safari 7 day cap applies
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: Small name and value pairs a site stores in the browser and gets back on every request.
nodes.m: The base identifier of the web: a random ID in a cookie lets a site recognise a returning browser, keep a login, and join visits into one profile. It is sent automatically with every matching request, so the person never has to act.
nodes.ps: Session cookie until browser closes, or up to 400 days in Chrome (cap since Chrome 104), 7 days for script set cookies in Safari
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.n: File System Access (read and write handles)
nodes.p: Lets a site open files and folders and save changes back in place.
nodes.m: Gives a site read and write access to specific files or directories the person picks. Since Chrome 122 a grant can persist across visits, so the site keeps access to your folder until revoked.
nodes.api: showOpenFilePicker(), showSaveFilePicker(), showDirectoryPicker(); handle.requestPermission({mode:'readwrite'}); IndexedDB stored handles
nodes.ui: Picker chooses what to share; a write prompt appears; Chrome 122 adds three-way prompt: Allow this time, Allow on every visit, Don't allow. Installed apps skip the prompt.
nodes.ps: One-time until tabs close, or persistent across visits in Chrome 122+ after Allow on every visit
nodes.rv: Address bar icon Remove access, Site settings per-handle trashcan; auto-revoked after a background period

nodes.p: A large browser database that can hold gigabytes of structured data for one site.
nodes.m: Stores app data, offline caches and, for trackers, bigger profiles or IDs that survive cookie clearing. Quota is a share of free disk, so a site can fill hundreds of MB without a prompt.
nodes.ps: Best effort: kept until the user clears it or the browser evicts under disk pressure. Safari applies the 7 day cap
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A browser store of up to about 5 MB per site that scripts read at any time and that survives restarts.
nodes.m: Holds settings, drafts, and very often a tracker's visitor ID that is re-created if the cookie is deleted. It is not sent to servers on its own, but every script on the page can read it. A common 'respawn' source for IDs.
nodes.ps: Until cleared by user or evicted. Safari deletes script written storage after 7 days of Safari use without a user visit
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A private, fast file area per site that the person cannot browse and that counts against quota.
nodes.m: Hosts SQLite or media caches in the browser. Invisible to the person in the file manager, uses the origin quota, and lasts until site data is cleared. Needs no prompt, unlike the File System Access picker.
nodes.ps: Same lifetime and quota as other origin storage
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A site can ask the browser to keep its data permanently; otherwise it can be evicted when disk is low.
nodes.m: navigator.storage.persist() asks for protected storage. Chrome grants it from engagement, bookmarks or install, Firefox asks the person. Best effort data is deleted least recently used first. storage.estimate() reveals quota, a coarse signal.
nodes.ui: Firefox shows a permission prompt, Chrome decides silently
nodes.ps: Persistent until cleared by the person. Best effort until eviction
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: Asks the browser not to delete this site's stored data under disk pressure.
nodes.m: Protects offline data (notes, drafts, downloaded media) from automatic eviction. Chrome and Safari decide silently from engagement; Firefox asks the person. A grant does not raise the quota.
nodes.ui: Firefox: bubble Store data in persistent storage, Allow or Don't allow. Chrome and Safari: no prompt, granted by heuristics (installed, bookmarked, notifications on, high engagement).
nodes.ps: Persistent until cleared by the person

nodes.p: Guesses whether the browser is in private mode using storage quota behavior.
nodes.m: Tells the site when someone is deliberately browsing privately. LinkedIn's script uses the FileSystem quota (Chrome 74 and older) or storage.estimate.

nodes.p: A per tab store of up to about 5 MB that is cleared when the tab closes.
nodes.m: Used for checkout steps and form state, and for trackers that carry a 'session ID' inside one tab. Different tabs of one site do not share it, so it cannot follow the person across tabs. Copied into a tab opened by window.open.
nodes.ps: Until the tab or window closes. Browsers may restore it after crash or tab restore
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A background script that all tabs of a site share, so one process keeps state across them.
nodes.m: Lets a site keep one connection and a single cross-tab state, which also shows how many tabs the person has. Partitioned like other storage in modern browsers, so a tracker cannot join sites with it.
nodes.ps: While at least one connected page is alive
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: Lets an embedded third-party frame ask for its own cookies back.
nodes.m: When third-party cookies are blocked, a frame can ask to use its first-party cookies. A grant lets that embed recognise the person across sites where it is embedded.
nodes.ui: Safari: always prompts (Allow or Don't Allow). Firefox: prompts after a number of sites; grants last 30 days. Chrome: prompts unless the sites are in the same Related Website Set (auto-grant).
nodes.ps: Per top-level site and embedded site pair; lapses after 30 days without interaction (Chrome and Firefox)
nodes.rv: Site settings, clearing site data, Permissions API 'change' event

nodes.n: Storage feature detection (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, openDatabase, addBehavior)
nodes.p: Tests which storage APIs work in this browser.
nodes.m: Support patterns show browser type and settings such as blocked storage. Old APIs (openDatabase, addBehavior) separate engines.
nodes.dm: Storage feature detection (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, openDatabase, addBehavior)

nodes.p: Browsers key embedded storage by the top site so a tracker sees a separate store on each site.
nodes.m: Cuts the main cross-site tracking path: a widget on site A and site B no longer shares one cookie or localStorage. Embeds can still track within one site, and workarounds shift to link decoration, redirects and server side IDs.
nodes.api: Browser behaviour keyed by (top-level site, frame site); use Storage Access API to opt out
nodes.ps: Per browser profile
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: How much each site may store on the device, per browser.
nodes.m: Caps how much a site can keep (IndexedDB, Cache, files). Large quotas let a site store gigabytes; quota values are derived from total disk size, so estimate() was padded to limit fingerprinting.
nodes.ui: No prompt; browser enforces quota and throws QuotaExceededError.
nodes.ps: Until evicted or cleared

nodes.p: Lets a top-level page request cookie access on behalf of related embedded sites.
nodes.m: Allows a page to unlock third-party cookies for sites in the same Related Website Set. Chrome only and deprecated; its use hints at cross-site identity joining.
nodes.ui: Chrome only: prompt unless the sites are in the same Related Website Set.
nodes.ps: Per top-level site

nodes.p: A string on the tab that survives page loads and was once used to carry data between sites.
nodes.m: Browsers now clear or partition it on cross-site navigation, so trackers can no longer hand an ID from one site to the next in a tab. Same-site use for session state still works. Large strings (MBs) were a legacy storage trick.
nodes.ps: Lives with the tab's browsing context
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: Safari deletes a site's script written storage after 7 days of Safari use without a visit to the site.
nodes.m: Covers localStorage, IndexedDB, Cache, service workers, media keys and script set cookies. The counter is days of Safari use, not calendar days. Installed Home Screen web apps are exempt. Limits long lived tracker storage.
nodes.ps: Deleted when Safari use passes 7 days with no user interaction on the site
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: What the person typed when signing up: name, email, phone, address, birthday and more.
nodes.m: Once signed in, every action ties to a stored identity. The site holds the typed fields plus order, device and login history. Email and phone are the keys ad platforms and data brokers use to match the person across services.
nodes.api: HTML forms with autocomplete tokens; server database
nodes.ps: Kept for the life of the account and usually for months after deletion for legal reasons
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A random Apple address that forwards mail to the person's real inbox.
nodes.m: A site sees random@privaterelay.appleid.com and cannot match the person across sites by email. Apple removes trackers inside forwarded mail only partly. The address stops working if the person deactivates it.
nodes.ps: Alias lasts until deactivated by the person
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A site recognises one person across phone, laptop and tablet when they sign in on each.
nodes.m: A shared login ID is a deterministic link. Hashed email, phone and shared IP add probabilistic links. Ad platforms with big login bases (Google, Meta, Apple) see the same person across devices; others rent graphs like UID2 or RampID.
nodes.api: Account ID in first party cookie or token; hashed email in ad requests
nodes.ps: Linked for as long as the account and ID graph entry exist
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A device held key that stops stolen session cookies from working on another computer.
nodes.m: The site gets short lived cookies refreshed with a signature from a key kept in the TPM or secure hardware. Reveals that the session is tied to one device. Chrome 146 on Windows (Apr 2026); GA for Google Workspace on May 25 2026.
nodes.api: Secure-Session-Registration and Secure-Session-Response headers; bound session cookie
nodes.ps: Cookie lifetime in minutes, refreshed by key proof until session ends
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A browser mediated sign in that works without third party cookies or hidden redirects.
nodes.m: The browser asks the identity provider for account data, shows a prompt, and only after consent shares the ID token with the site. Stops identity providers from tracking silently. Google is moving its sign in to FedCM.
nodes.ps: Browser remembers sign in state per account; revocable in site settings
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A page can ask whether this device can use a passkey, without showing a prompt.
nodes.m: Static checks such as PublicKeyCredential.isUserVerifyingPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable() and getClientCapabilities() say whether a built in authenticator, passkey autofill or a phone passkey is possible. Sites use them to decide what to show. The answers also reveal a headless server, virtual machine or container, whi
nodes.ps: Read fresh each time

nodes.p: Phishing resistant sign in with a key stored on the device or password manager.
nodes.m: The site gets a public key, a credential ID, a user handle and a signed challenge, not a secret. Attestation is usually withheld so the device model is not revealed. FIDO Alliance said in 2025 that over 15 billion accounts could use passkeys.
nodes.ui: Browser or OS prompt for passkey with biometric or PIN
nodes.ps: Credential lives in the authenticator until deleted; syncs through iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.n: Password manager and Credential Management API
nodes.p: Browsers and password managers fill saved logins and let a site read or store a credential.
nodes.m: A site learns the username the person chose, not the password manager's other entries. The Credential Management API lets a site request a saved credential after a gesture. Reused passwords across sites are the main account risk.
nodes.ps: Saved until the person deletes it in the password manager
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: The cookie or token that keeps a person signed in between pages.
nodes.m: A random session ID (OWASP: at least 64 bits of entropy) ties each request to an account. Whoever holds it is the person. Timeouts are 2 to 5 minutes idle for high risk apps and up to 30 minutes for low risk, per OWASP.
nodes.api: Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; __Host- prefix
nodes.ps: Session until browser close, or persistent up to 400 days. Idle and absolute server timeouts apply
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A login where Apple confirms identity and can hide the person's real email address.
nodes.m: Site gets a sub ID, email (real or relay) and email_verified; name only on first sign in. is_private_email and real_user_status (0 unsupported, 1 unknown, 2 likely real) are returned. Required in App Store apps that offer other social logins.
nodes.api: AppleID JS or redirect; OIDC id_token
nodes.ps: Authorisation lasts until the person revokes it in Apple Account settings
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A one click login where Google tells the site who the person is.
nodes.m: The site gets a signed ID token with sub (stable user ID), email, email_verified, name, picture, locale and for Workspace users the hd domain. Extra scopes can add Calendar, Drive or Contacts. The site gets the same sub every visit.
nodes.api: Google Identity Services: google.accounts.id.initialize(); OIDC id_token
nodes.ps: Google session cookies keep the person signed in; site stores its own session
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A login where LinkedIn confirms the person and shares basic professional profile details.
nodes.m: With scopes openid, profile and email the site gets sub, name, given_name, family_name, picture, locale, email and email_verified in an ID token. Work history and connections need separate approved partner APIs.
nodes.api: OIDC authorization code flow at linkedin.com/oauth/v2/authorization
nodes.ps: Access tokens last about 60 days; refresh tokens up to 1 year for approved apps (verify)
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A login where Microsoft Entra or a personal account tells the site who the person is.
nodes.m: ID token claims include sub, oid (directory object ID), tid (tenant ID), name, preferred_username and optionally email. Work accounts reveal the employer's tenant ID. Graph scopes can add mail, files and calendar.
nodes.ps: Refresh tokens last up to 90 days for work accounts by default
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: Test tools can add a pretend passkey device to a browser so sign in flows run without hardware.
nodes.m: The WebAuthn spec defines a WebDriver extension for virtual authenticators. Chrome exposes it through the DevTools Protocol WebAuthn domain and Selenium and Playwright expose it to scripts. A test or agent can register and use passkeys with no phone or security key. A site cannot call this from a page; it is a tool lev
nodes.api: WebDriver Virtual Authenticator commands; CDP WebAuthn.addVirtualAuthenticator, addCredential, setUserVerified
nodes.ui: None; only the driver can turn it on
nodes.ps: For the test session

nodes.p: A computer shows a QR code and your phone approves the passkey sign in.
nodes.m: Hybrid transport lets a passkey on a phone sign you in on another device. The computer shows a QR code, the phone scans it, and the two devices check they are near each other over Bluetooth before talking through a relay. It works on a browser with no passkey of its own. An unattended cloud browser or agent cannot fini
nodes.api: navigator.credentials.get({publicKey}) with hybrid transport chosen in the browser's passkey sheet; transport value 'hybrid'
nodes.ui: Browser passkey sheet with QR code, then phone prompt
nodes.ps: Per site and passkey
nodes.rv: Delete the passkey on the phone or in the password manager

nodes.p: A site can ask the browser to present a certificate stored on the computer.
nodes.m: Certificates identify a person or company. The browser asks which cert to send; used in banks and enterprise.
nodes.api: TLS CertificateRequest during handshake; browser certificate chooser
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: A site can ask the browser to present a certificate stored on the computer.

nodes.p: Lets a site store and fetch saved passwords through the browser.
nodes.m: Gets a stored username and password after the person picks an account, without scraping form fields.
nodes.ui: Account chooser sheet; auto sign in option
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets a site store and fetch saved passwords through the browser.

nodes.n: Digital Credentials API (mDL and wallet IDs)
nodes.p: Lets a site ask for a government ID or other credential from a digital wallet.
nodes.m: Requests only fields the person approves (age over 21, name, address) from a wallet such as Google Wallet or Apple Wallet, with a browser prompt.
nodes.ui: Browser wallet picker plus per field consent in the wallet
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets a site ask for a government ID or other credential from a digital wallet.

nodes.p: Lets a site ask the browser to sign the person in with Google, Apple or similar without third party cookies.
nodes.m: Gives the site an ID token for a chosen identity provider account; the browser mediates the prompt.
nodes.ui: Browser account chooser (passive in the page or active after a click)
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets a site ask the browser to sign the person in with Google, Apple or similar without third party cookies.

nodes.p: A server can make the browser ask for a username and password.
nodes.m: Browser shows a native login box and then sends credentials on every request to that realm.
nodes.api: WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm=...; Authorization header; Negotiate/NTLM for Windows SSO
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: A server can make the browser ask for a username and password.

nodes.p: Lets a site sign people in with their LinkedIn account and receive basic profile data.
nodes.m: After the person approves, the site gets a stable pairwise ID, name, photo, locale and optionally a verified email. It does not verify real world identity.
nodes.ps: Access token lifetime set by LinkedIn; consent until revoked in LinkedIn settings

nodes.p: Lets one site share a trust signal about a visitor with another without identifying them.
nodes.m: Carries a one bit trust token to other origins so bots can be told from people without a login. Privacy Sandbox wind down affects its future.
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets one site share a trust signal about a visitor with another without identifying them.

nodes.p: Lets an embedded iframe ask for its own cookies back on third party pages.
nodes.m: Restores a login cookie inside an embed with a browser prompt. Used for SSO widgets and embedded apps.
nodes.ui: Browser prompt to let embedded site use cookies on the host site
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets an embedded iframe ask for its own cookies back on third party pages.

nodes.p: Creates a passkey or security key credential for the site.
nodes.m: Makes a public key login bound to the site's domain. The site never sees the private key or biometrics.
nodes.ui: OS or browser sheet: use Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello, phone or security key
nodes.ps: Credential persists on authenticator or cloud keychain
nodes.rv: Delete passkey in OS password manager; signalUnknownCredential from the site
nodes.dm: Creates a passkey or security key credential for the site.

nodes.p: Signs the person in with a passkey, including autofill style suggestions.
nodes.m: Proves who the person is without a password. Conditional UI shows passkeys in the username field.

nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Signs the person in with a passkey, including autofill style suggestions.

nodes.p: Derives a secret from a passkey or stores a small blob on it.
nodes.m: Lets an app use the passkey as a key for end to end encryption (PRF is a 32 byte HMAC output). largeBlob stores small data on the authenticator.
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Derives a secret from a passkey or stores a small blob on it.

nodes.p: Lets one passkey work across several of a company's domains.
nodes.m: Allows an RP ID to be shared by listed sites so passkeys follow brand domains. Limited labels prevent abuse.
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets one passkey work across several of a company's domains.

nodes.p: Lets a site tell the passkey manager a credential is gone or its name changed.
nodes.m: Keeps the passkey list clean. Shows no data back to the site.
nodes.ps: Per origin
nodes.dm: Lets a site tell the passkey manager a credential is gone or its name changed.

nodes.p: Asks to read what is on the clipboard.
nodes.m: Can show anything the person copied: passwords, addresses, personal messages. Chromium asks permission; Firefox and Safari show a one-time Paste menu so the person approves each read.
nodes.ui: Chromium: permission prompt when document is focused. Firefox 125+ and Safari: floating Paste menu available after 1 second, skipped for same-origin content.
nodes.ps: Chromium: persistent per origin; Firefox and Safari: none

nodes.p: Puts text or images onto the clipboard.
nodes.m: Can overwrite what the person copied, for example swapping a crypto address. Allowed on a click without a prompt in all browsers.
nodes.ui: No prompt; needs transient activation or (Chromium) the clipboard-write permission, which is auto-granted to the active tab.
nodes.ps: Per call

nodes.p: Makes any element editable; the browser spellcheck may run on what is typed.
nodes.m: A site can build rich editors from plain HTML. With a cloud assisted spellcheck on, typed text can leave the device, so editing in a web page is not always private.
nodes.api: contenteditable=true|plaintext-only; spellcheck attribute; document.execCommand (legacy); Selection and Range
nodes.ps: While the element exists
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.n: Copy and cut events (rewrite what gets copied)
nodes.p: Lets a page change what the person's copy or cut puts on the clipboard.
nodes.m: When the person presses copy, the site can append a credit line, strip formatting, or substitute other text. It cannot see other apps' copies; it only controls copies made inside its own page.
nodes.ps: Per copy action
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Lets canvas or custom editors receive IME and keyboard text input without a hidden text box.
nodes.m: A page can run its own editor surface and still get full IME and emoji input. It sees the same typing data as a normal text field, so the privacy picture is unchanged.
nodes.api: new EditContext(); element.editContext = ctx; textupdate, textformatupdate, characterboundsupdate
nodes.ps: While attached
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Every click and key event says whether the browser made it or a script made it.
nodes.m: Event.isTrusted is true for events created by the browser from real input and false for events a page script creates with dispatchEvent or element.click(). Agents that drive the browser through the DevTools Protocol send input the browser treats as real, so they pass. Agents that script clicks inside the page fail.

nodes.p: Sees every key pressed while the page has focus, plus IME composition text.
nodes.m: A page that has focus gets each keydown with the key and its physical code, and exact timing. Typing rhythm can identify a person; composition events reveal the language they type in.
nodes.api: keydown, keyup, beforeinput, input, compositionstart/update/end; KeyboardEvent.key, .code, .timeStamp
nodes.ps: While the document has focus
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Reads which character each physical key makes, so the page can tell the keyboard layout.
nodes.m: The layout map shows if the person types on QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak or a language specific keyboard. That narrows country and language, and helps shortcuts, but it is also a fingerprint hint.
nodes.ps: One-shot per call
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
nodes.dm: Map of key code to produced character

nodes.p: Captures keys like Escape and Alt+Tab while in fullscreen.
nodes.m: Lets games and remote desktops receive keys the browser normally keeps, so a site can trap Escape or Ctrl+W. Works only in fullscreen; a long-press of Escape always exits.
nodes.ui: No prompt; works only while the page is in fullscreen.
nodes.ps: While in fullscreen

nodes.p: Reveals the physical-to-printed key mapping, i.e. the keyboard layout.
nodes.m: Shows which keyboard layout the person uses (QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak, language), a strong locale and fingerprint signal. No prompt.
nodes.ui: No prompt; Chromium exposes it to secure contexts.
nodes.ps: n/a

nodes.p: Asks to list every font installed on the device.
nodes.m: Reveals the full list of installed fonts and raw font files, which identifies the device and installed software. Gated by prompt because font lists were a long-standing fingerprint.
nodes.ui: Chrome prompt: See fonts on your device, Allow or Block; needs a gesture.
nodes.ps: Persistent per origin

nodes.n: Paste event (read what the person pastes)
nodes.p: Gives the page the clipboard contents, but only when the person presses paste inside the page.
nodes.m: A paste is consent for that one read: the site gets text, HTML or files the person chose to paste. It cannot peek at the clipboard at other times, which blocks silent snooping.
nodes.ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
nodes.ps: Per paste action
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Reports pointer position and, for pens and touch, pressure, tilt and contact size.
nodes.m: Mouse paths, speed and hesitation are strong behavioral signals (bot detection, attention tracking). Pen and touch fields add pressure and tilt that can tell devices apart.
nodes.api: pointerdown/move/up; PointerEvent.pressure, tiltX, tiltY, width, height, pointerType; getCoalescedEvents(); pointerrawupdate
nodes.ps: While the pointer is over the page
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Hides and captures the mouse for games and 3D views.
nodes.m: Gives raw relative mouse movement with unlimited range while the cursor is hidden. With unadjustedMovement the site gets unaccelerated input, a small hardware hint.
nodes.ui: Browser shows an on-screen notice and Esc to exit; some platforms prompt on re-lock. Needs a gesture.
nodes.ps: Until Esc or unlock
nodes.du: per mouse event (about 125 Hz or higher)

nodes.p: Lets the page see what is selected inside itself and move the cursor; nothing outside the page.
nodes.m: A site knows which of its own words the person highlights, which reveals interest and reading focus. It cannot see a selection in another tab or app.
nodes.ps: Live while the page has focus
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Clicks and keys sent by a tool tend to be too neat, too fast or oddly placed.
nodes.m: Input sent through the DevTools Protocol is trusted, so defenses look at how it behaves. Common tells are a click with no earlier mouse move, exact element center targets, whole number coordinates, identical gaps between keys, and zero hold time between key down and key up. Some tools also gave screen coordinates that
nodes.api: mousemove/pointermove/click timing; MouseEvent.clientX/screenX; KeyboardEvent timing; PointerEvent.getCoalescedEvents()

nodes.n: Touch events and touch point count
nodes.p: Reports finger positions and the number of touch points the device supports.
nodes.m: navigator.maxTouchPoints separates phones, tablets and touch laptops from plain desktops, a common fingerprint input. Touch radius and force add small device level detail.
nodes.api: touchstart/move/end; Touch.radiusX, radiusY, force; navigator.maxTouchPoints; 'ontouchstart' in window
nodes.ps: While touching
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Lets a page control whether the on-screen keyboard resizes the page or overlays it, and show or hide it.
nodes.m: A web app can take over keyboard layout handling and learn the keyboard rectangle. Keyboard height hints at device type and which keyboard (emoji, numeric) is open.
nodes.api: navigator.virtualKeyboard.overlaysContent; show(); hide(); boundingRect; geometrychange; env(keyboard-inset-height); virtualkeyboardpolicy
nodes.ps: While the page runs
nodes.rv: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)

nodes.p: Ordered list of the person's preferred languages, sent on every request.
nodes.m: Shows native language, second languages and country (en-US vs en-GB, es-419). A multilingual list narrows identity sharply: 5.9 bits in 2016. Sites localize with it; trackers fingerprint it.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Combining contrast, motion, forced colors, zoom and font size to guess a disability.
nodes.m: No single API says disabled, but together prefers-contrast, forced-colors, reduced-motion, large fonts and zoom flag vision, vestibular or motor needs. Under GDPR or similar this may be special-category data.
nodes.api: Combination of CSS media queries, zoom and font size
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Header and property saying the person asked not to be tracked; mostly ignored.
nodes.m: Reveals a privacy preference (about 1 in 4 desktop Chrome and Firefox users enabled it at its peak) and ironically adds a fingerprint bit. Safari removed it in 12.1; Firefox is removing the setting.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Browser signal that the person opts out of sale or sharing of data.
nodes.m: Legally binding opt-out in California, Colorado, Connecticut and more, so sites must honor it. Also tells the site this user runs privacy-focused settings or a browser like Firefox, DuckDuckGo or Brave.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Number, date, calendar, numbering system and hour cycle formats the browser would use.
nodes.m: resolvedOptions() exposes calendar (gregory, buddhist, japanese), numberingSystem (latn, arab), hourCycle (h12 or h23), and decimal and thousands marks. Reveals regional OS settings beyond language.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Which character each physical key produces, revealing QWERTY, AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak etc.
nodes.m: Tells native keyboard layout and so likely country and language (French AZERTY, German QWERTZ, Colemak enthusiasts). Chromium returns about 48 key codes, no prompt.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Reads the language the browser asks pages to use.
nodes.m: Reveals language, region and sometimes nationality. Order of preferred languages narrows identity.

nodes.p: IANA time zone name plus UTC offset from Intl and Date.
nodes.m: Narrows physical location to a region (about 400 IANA zones; America/Chicago). Mismatch with IP location is a VPN tell. 3 bits at the offset level, more with the full zone name.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.n: Browser zoom and default text size
nodes.p: Infers page zoom and the person's default font size from layout measurements.
nodes.m: Zoom (50% to 500%) from devicePixelRatio and window size; default font size (usually 16 px, but 12 to 24 px settable) from computed em. Large values suggest low vision or older users.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Reads whether the person turned on Do Not Track.
nodes.m: A setting few sites honor; LinkedIn says it does not generally respond to it. The collector reads it but excludes it from the hash.

nodes.p: Tilt and shake data from the phone; iOS asks first, Android Chrome does not.
nodes.m: Reveals how the device is held and moved: tilt, walking cadence, vehicle vibration. Research has inferred PINs and keystrokes from tilt patterns, and it hints at device class.
nodes.ui: iOS Safari 13+: system alert asking for Motion and Orientation access, Allow or Don't Allow, after requestPermission(). Chrome and Firefox on Android: no prompt, Motion sensors site setting defaults to Allow. Most desktops: events do not fi
nodes.ps: iOS: remembered for the page session and re-asked after the page process ends; Chrome: site setting Allow or Block per origin
nodes.rv: iOS: Settings > Safari > Advanced > Motion & Orientation Access (iOS 12.2 global switch); Chrome: Site settings > Motion sensors

nodes.p: A browser-drawn button that asks for location; the click itself is the request.
nodes.m: Same data as Geolocation, but the request starts from a trusted button the site cannot disguise, so prompts only appear when the person asked. Chrome can also re-ask after a block.
nodes.api: <geolocation autolocate accuracymode="precise|approximate" watch onlocation=...>; element.position, element.error
nodes.ui: Browser-drawn button with fixed text and icon; a click opens the normal location prompt, re-reads silently if already granted, and offers a recovery path if blocked.
nodes.ps: Same stored geolocation permission as the script API
nodes.du: one-shot, or continuous with the watch attribute

nodes.p: Lets an embedded frame ask for location only if the parent page allows it.
nodes.m: Controls whether ad, map or widget frames can see where the person is. The default blocks cross-origin frames so third parties cannot request location through a host page.
nodes.ui: Same prompt as top-level, worded for the top-level site; the grant is delegated to the iframe origin.
nodes.ps: Per top-level origin; delegated frames share the top-level grant
nodes.rv: Same site settings entry as the top-level origin

nodes.p: Asks the person for their device location, precise or approximate.
nodes.m: Tells the site where the person physically is, down to a few meters outdoors: home, workplace, travel, daily routine. Repeated fixes reveal patterns of life.
nodes.api: navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(), watchPosition(), clearWatch(); options enableHighAccuracy, timeout, maximumAge
nodes.ui: Chrome: bubble with Allow while visiting, Allow this time (Chrome 116), Don't allow. Firefox: Allow or Block with optional Remember. Safari: Allow or Don't Allow. Android 12+: Precise or Approximate choice. OS Location Services must also be
nodes.ps: Chrome and Edge: persistent per origin after Allow; Allow this time ends when the tab closes or is backgrounded. Firefox: permanent only if Remember is ticked. Safari: asks again per visit unless set to Allow.
nodes.rv: Padlock and Site settings; Chrome Safety Check auto-resets unused permissions; PermissionStatus 'change' event; turning off OS Location Services blocks all sites.
nodes.dm: Coordinates with accuracy radius and optional speed and heading
nodes.du: one-shot, or continuous via watchPosition (about 1 update per second on GPS)

nodes.p: Reads device acceleration, with or without gravity, as a stream.
nodes.m: Shows how the phone moves and rests: walking cadence, vehicle vibration, on a table or in a pocket. Sensor noise can fingerprint the hardware.
nodes.api: new Accelerometer({frequency, referenceFrame}); new LinearAccelerationSensor(); new GravitySensor()
nodes.ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.
nodes.ps: Site setting Allow or Block per origin
nodes.dm: Sensor readings at the requested frequency

nodes.p: Reads the light level (lux) around the device; not shipped by default anywhere.
nodes.m: Shows whether the person is indoors, outdoors or in a dark room. Research showed it can leak visited links and cross-origin pixels, so Chrome keeps it behind a flag and Firefox removed it.
nodes.ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.
nodes.ps: Site setting Allow or Block per origin
nodes.dm: Sensor readings at the requested frequency

nodes.p: Reads how fast the device is rotating around three axes.
nodes.m: Shows how fast the device turns. Gyroscope noise has been used to eavesdrop on nearby speech (Gyrophone, 2014) and to fingerprint devices, which is why browsers cap the rate.
nodes.ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.
nodes.ps: Site setting Allow or Block per origin
nodes.dm: Sensor readings at the requested frequency

nodes.p: Reads the magnetic field around the device, like a compass.
nodes.m: Gives compass heading and can reveal nearby metal and electronics. Indoor magnetic fields form a rough fingerprint of a building or room.
nodes.ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.
nodes.ps: Site setting Allow or Block per origin
nodes.dm: Sensor readings at the requested frequency

nodes.p: Fused device orientation as a quaternion or rotation matrix.
nodes.m: Gives exact device attitude relative to Earth (absolute) or to its start pose (relative). Same privacy class as DeviceOrientation but easier to use for 3D scenes.
nodes.api: new AbsoluteOrientationSensor({frequency}); new RelativeOrientationSensor(); quaternion; populateMatrix()
nodes.ui: Chromium shows no bubble: access follows the Motion sensors site setting (default Allow) plus the Permissions API name. Safari and Firefox do not ship the API.
nodes.ps: Site setting Allow or Block per origin

nodes.p: AI crawlers and browsing agents often announce themselves by name in the User-Agent header.
nodes.m: Operators publish names such as GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, Claude-User, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended. Many split them into training crawlers, search crawlers and fetchers that run when a person asks a question. Sites can allow or block them in robots.txt (RFC 9309). A name is only a claim unle
nodes.api: User-Agent request header; robots.txt product tokens (RFC 9309)

nodes.p: The IP maps to an ISP or hosting company, which tells if the visitor is a home, mobile or cloud user.
nodes.m: ASN databases label IPs as residential, mobile, business, hosting or education. Datacenter ASNs (AWS, GCP, OVH) trigger bot and fraud rules. Residential proxies are harder to spot.
nodes.api: BGP origin ASN lookup; IPinfo or MaxMind ASN and Anonymous IP databases

nodes.p: Anti-bot services combine many browser and network signals to guess if the visitor is automated.
nodes.m: Inputs include navigator.webdriver, headless user agents and CDP side effects, JA3/JA4 and HTTP/2 mismatches, canvas and WebGL consistency, mouse and key timing, IP reputation and challenge solving (Turnstile, reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha).
nodes.api: navigator.webdriver; challenge scripts; fingerprints; Privacy Pass tokens

nodes.p: Servers ask the browser for extra device details through request headers.
nodes.m: A server sends Accept-CH to receive hints such as Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version, Arch, Bitness, Model, Device-Memory, DPR and Viewport-Width. Critical-CH forces a retry with them. Chromium only; Firefox and Safari do not send them.
nodes.api: Accept-CH and Critical-CH response headers; Sec-CH-* request headers

nodes.p: Every request carries the sender's public IP address.
nodes.m: The server sees the IP (or the proxy or relay address). IPv4 gives about 32 bits at most; an IPv6 /64 gives up to 64. It is the base for geolocation, ISP and VPN checks, and rate limits. Shared NAT and CGNAT blur it.
nodes.api: TCP/IP source address; X-Forwarded-For at proxies

nodes.p: A page makes the browser look up unique hostnames so the site learns which DNS resolver the visitor uses.
nodes.m: The page requests random-subdomain.example. The authoritative server logs which recursive resolver asked, revealing the ISP, a public DNS (Google, Cloudflare), or a VPN leak. DoH hides it from the local network, not from the site.
nodes.api: fetch/img to unique subdomains; authoritative DNS logging

nodes.p: Encrypted Client Hello and DNS over HTTPS hide which site a visitor connects to from the local network.
nodes.m: ECH encrypts the SNI and the rest of the ClientHello using a key from DNS HTTPS records (RFC 9849 in Chrome 117 and Firefox 118 era). DoH encrypts DNS lookups. They hide hostnames from ISPs but not from the site, and they weaken JA3/JA4 on the wire.
nodes.api: TLS ECH extension; HTTPS RR; DoH

nodes.p: A tracker stores an ID in the cache validators of a file, which come back on every request.
nodes.m: A server sets a unique ETag or Last-Modified on a resource; the browser sends If-None-Match back, identifying the visitor. Since cache partitioning (Chrome 86, Firefox 85, Safari earlier) the ID is only valid per top-level site.

nodes.p: A site encodes an ID into which favicons were cached, which survives clearing cookies.
nodes.m: NDSS 2021 (Solomos et al.) showed a persistent ID stored in the favicon cache across subdomains, surviving cookie clearing and even private browsing in some browsers. Vendors patched after disclosure.
nodes.api: Favicon requests to N subdomain paths; navigation redirect probing

nodes.p: A site stores an ID in which subdomains the browser has been told to load only over HTTPS.
nodes.m: Each bit is a subdomain set to HSTS or not. The tracker reads it back by probing http:// URLs and seeing which upgrade (Kamkar 2015). Safari's ITP and clearing site data restrict it; HSTS is mostly cleared with history.
nodes.api: Strict-Transport-Security on N subdomains; redirect probing
nodes.dm: N bit identifier (a few dozen subdomains)

nodes.p: The set and order of request headers is different for each browser and HTTP library.
nodes.m: Chrome, Firefox and Safari send Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding and Sec-* headers in distinct orders; scripted clients (requests, Go, Node fetch) differ. Mismatches versus the User-Agent flag bots.

nodes.p: HTTP/2 settings, window updates and header order differ by browser and are readable by the server.
nodes.m: Akamai's fingerprint (Black Hat EU 2017) joins SETTINGS values, WINDOW_UPDATE, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order. Chrome sends m,a,s,p, Firefox m,p,a,s and Safari m,s,p,a; Go and Python clients differ visibly.
nodes.api: HTTP/2 frame capture at the edge

nodes.p: QUIC's first packet carries a readable ClientHello, giving the same fingerprints as TLS plus transport parameters.
nodes.m: The QUIC Initial packet is encrypted with a public key, so middleboxes can read the TLS ClientHello and QUIC transport parameters. JA4 has a QUIC variant (prefix q). Connection ID length and version also differ per stack.
nodes.api: QUIC Initial packet decrypt at edge; JA4 q variant

nodes.p: The server converts the visitor's IP into an approximate country, region and city.
nodes.m: Commercial databases (MaxMind, IPinfo, IP2Location) map IPs to places. Vendors claim about 99.8% country accuracy, but city accuracy is much lower and mobile or VPN IPs often point to the carrier hub or exit.
nodes.api: GeoIP lookup of the client IP (MaxMind GeoIP2, IPinfo)
nodes.dm: Country, region, city, lat and long with accuracy radius

nodes.n: IP masking (Private Relay, IP Protection, Tor)
nodes.p: Some browsers route traffic through relays so sites do not see the visitor's real IP.
nodes.m: iCloud Private Relay (Safari, iCloud+ subscribers) uses two hops with a coarse egress location. Chrome IP Protection proxies selected third-party traffic in Incognito for known trackers. Tor routes everything over 3 hops.
nodes.api: OHTTP-style multi-hop relays; MASQUE; Tor circuits

nodes.n: IPv6 prefix and interface ID stability
nodes.p: IPv6 addresses can stay stable for weeks, making them a long lived ID even if cookies are cleared.
nodes.m: The /64 prefix delegated by an ISP often persists for weeks or months, while privacy extensions rotate the interface ID (about daily). Servers key on the /64 or /56 to identify a household.

nodes.p: The TLS handshake order of ciphers and extensions identifies the client software.
nodes.m: JA3 (Salesforce, 2017) is an MD5 of version, ciphers, extensions, curves and point formats in the ClientHello. Chrome 110 randomized extension order (Jan 2023), so one browser now yields many JA3s; JA4 sorts them out.
nodes.api: TLS ClientHello parsing at CDN or server

nodes.p: A newer family of fingerprints for TLS, HTTP, TCP and more, built to survive randomization.
nodes.m: JA4 (FoxIO, 2023) sorts ciphers and extensions so Chrome's shuffle gives one value. JA4S (server), JA4H (HTTP), JA4L (latency), JA4X (cert), JA4SSH and JA4T (TCP) extend it. JA4 is BSD licensed; the rest use FoxIO License 1.1.

nodes.p: Chrome asks the user before a public website can reach devices on their local network.
nodes.m: Chrome 142 added a prompt for requests to private IPs. Chrome 145 split it into local-network and loopback-network permissions, and 147 extended it to WebSocket and WebTransport. It replaced Private Network Access preflights.
nodes.ui: Look for and connect to any device on your local network

nodes.p: A page probes ports on the visitor's own machine or home network to find running software.
nodes.m: JavaScript uses fetch, WebSocket or image timing to test localhost ports (eBay's 2020 check, Meta Pixel and Yandex on Android in 2025 messaging via localhost). Chrome LNA prompts since 142 and PNA aim to stop this.
nodes.api: fetch/WebSocket/img to 127.0.0.1 and RFC1918 hosts; timing

nodes.p: A signed token proves the visitor is probably a real device without revealing who they are.
nodes.m: Privacy Pass (RFC 9576 to 9578) tokens issued after device or account attestation. Apple PAT ships in Safari and Cloudflare Turnstile consumes tokens. PACT was announced on 2026-06-22 by Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and Shopify; Apple was not listed.
nodes.api: Privacy Pass PrivateToken challenge in WWW-Authenticate; PAT

nodes.p: Requests tell the destination site which page the visitor came from.
nodes.m: The default policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin (Chrome 85, Firefox 87) sends only the origin cross-site. Safari has capped cross-site referrers to the origin since 12.1. Full URLs still go same-site.
nodes.api: Referer and Origin request headers; Referrer-Policy; document.referrer

nodes.n: Reverse DNS (PTR) of the client IP
nodes.p: A reverse lookup of the IP can return an ISP hostname that hints at location or line type.
nodes.m: PTR records such as pool-1-2-3-4.nycmny.fios.verizon.net expose ISP, city codes and sometimes dynamic vs static addressing. Servers do this for logs and bot checks (Googlebot verification).
nodes.api: DNS PTR lookup for in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa

nodes.n: Sec-CH-UA low entropy hints and reduced User-Agent
nodes.p: Chromium sends brand, mobile flag and platform in every request by default, with a frozen User-Agent string.
nodes.m: Sec-CH-UA lists browser brands and major versions (with a GREASE brand), Sec-CH-UA-Mobile and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. The User-Agent string is frozen to a reduced form in Chrome 110 and later.
nodes.api: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile, Sec-CH-UA-Platform request headers; navigator.userAgentData

nodes.p: Browsers add headers saying where a request came from and why, which servers use to block cross-site abuse.
nodes.m: Sec-Fetch-Site, Mode, Dest and User tell the server if a request is same-origin, a navigation, or user triggered. They are not user identifying but help servers tell real browsers from scripts.

nodes.p: The TCP handshake reveals the operating system through TTL, window size, MSS and option order.
nodes.m: p0f (Zalewski) and JA4T read SYN fields: initial TTL (64 or 128), window size, MSS, window scale and option order. Windows, Linux, iOS and macOS differ, and a mismatch with the User-Agent signals spoofing or a proxy.
nodes.api: SYN packet capture (p0f v3, JA4T, Zeek)

nodes.p: Reuse of a TLS session ticket can link a visitor's connections across sites that share a server.
nodes.m: A session ticket or PSK is a stable ID, so two domains behind one CDN or server can see the same resumption. Sy et al. (ACSAC 2018) found browsers reusing tickets across origins. Chrome partitioned TLS session caches by network isolation key.
nodes.api: TLS 1.2 session tickets, TLS 1.3 PSK; session ID

nodes.p: Sites guess whether the visitor hides behind a VPN, proxy or Tor.
nodes.m: Methods: IP lists (Tor exit list, hosting ASNs), latency versus claimed geography, timezone and language versus IP, WebRTC leaks, open ports, MTU and TCP quirks. Residential VPN IPs often slip through.
nodes.api: IP reputation; Tor bulk exit list; RTT triangulation; timezone mismatch

nodes.p: An agent can sign its web requests so a site can check who sent them.
nodes.m: Web Bot Auth uses HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). The agent adds Signature, Signature-Input and a Signature-Agent header that points to a public key directory. The site fetches the keys and verifies the signature, so a user agent name cannot be faked. Google lists it as experimental for its own agent, and cloud age
nodes.api: Signature, Signature-Input and Signature-Agent request headers; key directory at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory

nodes.p: WebRTC used to expose the device's local network IP; browsers now hide it behind a random .local name.
nodes.m: RTCPeerConnection gathers ICE host candidates. Since 2019 and 2020 Chrome and Firefox replace private IPs with mDNS .local names, but granting getUserMedia (camera or microphone) restores real addresses.

nodes.p: A STUN request lets a page discover the public IP of the real network path, even behind some VPNs.
nodes.m: ICE gathering sends UDP to a STUN server and learns the server reflexive address. Proxies and browser VPN extensions that cannot proxy UDP leak the real IP. Chrome WebRTC IP handling policies and Brave default settings block this.

nodes.p: Reads estimated connection speed, type and latency.
nodes.m: Reveals if the person is on Wi-Fi, cellular or slow links; changes over time so useful for short term session linking.

nodes.p: Opt-in headers carrying DPR, viewport width, device memory and color scheme.
nodes.m: Sec-CH-DPR, Sec-CH-Viewport-Width, Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-Device-Memory and Sec-CH-Prefers-Color-Scheme let servers pick image sizes and themes before first paint, and also hand the same fingerprint bits to every server that asks.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Raw TCP and UDP sockets from a page, for installed isolated apps only.
nodes.m: Lets an installed Isolated Web App open arbitrary TCP and UDP connections and servers. Not available to normal websites because it would bypass same-origin and CORS protections.
nodes.api: new TCPSocket(host, port); new UDPSocket(); new TCPServerSocket(); policies direct-sockets, direct-sockets-private
nodes.ui: Only inside Isolated Web Apps (signed bundles); IWA install prompt; permission policy direct-sockets, plus direct-sockets-private for LAN ranges.
nodes.ps: Tied to the installed app

nodes.p: Server-side headers with the effective connection type, RTT and downlink.
nodes.m: Same numbers as the Network Information API but delivered on requests so the server can adapt before sending HTML. Requires Accept-CH opt-in, with the same 25 ms and 25 kbps rounding.
nodes.api: Accept-CH: ECT, RTT, Downlink; request headers ECT, RTT, Downlink
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Asks to let a public site talk to devices on your home or office network.
nodes.m: Blocks a public website from reaching private IP addresses (printers, routers, smart devices) unless you allow it. Closes the old way for sites to scan or attack your LAN from the browser.
nodes.ui: Chrome prompt: Look for and connect to any device on your local network, Allow or Block. Applies to subresource requests from public sites to private IPs.
nodes.ps: Persistent per origin until reset

nodes.p: Asks to let a public site talk to services on this very computer.
nodes.m: Controls access to localhost services (dev servers, local agents, desktop apps). Sites used to probe localhost ports to detect installed software, so access now needs consent.
nodes.ui: Chrome prompt for requests from public sites to 127.0.0.1 or localhost. Legacy name local-network-access still accepted as an alias.
nodes.ps: Persistent per origin

nodes.p: Estimated connection type, speed and latency, plus a data-saver flag.
nodes.m: Lets a site pick light pages on slow links. effectiveType buckets: slow-2g, 2g, 3g, 4g. downlink rounds to 25 kbps steps (capped near 10 Mbps), rtt to 25 ms steps. Type (wifi or cellular) is Android only.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Tells the page whether the device believes it has a network.
nodes.m: Boolean only; true can still mean a captive portal or no internet. Events fire when the device loses or regains connection, revealing travel, elevators, flights.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Request header showing the person turned on data saving.
nodes.m: Save-Data: on indicates Lite mode on a metered or slow connection, often in lower-income or roaming contexts. Sites should send lighter pages.
nodes.ps: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored

nodes.p: Uses a WebRTC peer connection to learn the device's local and public IP addresses.
nodes.m: Can reveal a real IP behind a VPN and LAN addresses. Browsers now often hide local addresses behind mDNS names. LinkedIn uses stun.l.google.com:19302 and an IP regex.

nodes.p: Downloads large files after the person leaves, with a progress notification.
nodes.m: Lets a site download or upload big files outside the tab. The browser shows progress UI so the person can see and cancel it.
nodes.ui: No prompt; Chrome shows a persistent progress notification the person can cancel.
nodes.ps: Per fetch

nodes.p: Retries a request later when the connection returns, after the tab closes.
nodes.m: Lets a site send queued data (a message, a form, a like) once the device is back online even if the person has left. Quiet and automatic, so no prompt is shown.
nodes.ui: No prompt; the Permissions API reports background-sync as always granted.
nodes.ps: Tied to the service worker registration
nodes.rv: Unregister the service worker or clear site data

nodes.p: Shows a number or dot on an installed app icon.
nodes.m: Puts an unread count on the app icon of an installed web app. No prompt on desktop, but iOS needs notification permission and an installed app. It shows the person that the app has attention to give.
nodes.ui: No prompt on desktop Chrome and Edge; iOS requires Home Screen web app plus granted notifications.
nodes.ps: Persists until cleared

nodes.p: Tells a site when the person is away from keyboard and mouse or the screen is locked.
nodes.m: Reveals when the person is present: active or idle (at least 60 seconds) and whether the screen is locked. Useful for chat presence; also shows daily schedule, sleep and work hours.
nodes.ui: Chrome prompt Know when you are actively using your device, Allow or Block; needs a user gesture.
nodes.ps: Persistent per origin

nodes.p: Scheduled local notifications that fire without a server; not shipped.
nodes.m: Would have let a site schedule notifications for a future time without push. Chrome ran an origin trial and then dropped it, so no browser ships it.
nodes.ui: Needed notification permission plus an origin trial token.
nodes.ps: Per scheduled notification

nodes.p: Asks to show system notifications outside the browser tab.
nodes.m: Lets a site put messages on the person's desktop or lock screen. Reaches the person after they leave the page; abuse is spam, scams and fake alerts, so browsers add quiet prompts and auto-revocation.
nodes.ui: Chrome: bubble with Allow or Block, or a quiet address-bar chip (Notifications blocked) from Chrome 80 for sites people rarely allow. Firefox: Allow or Not now plus Always block, needs a gesture since 72. Safari: system sheet, needs a gestu
nodes.ps: Persistent per origin; Chrome auto-revokes unused or abusive sites and tells the person; Safari ties to the Notification Center
nodes.rv: Padlock, Site settings, OS notification settings, Safety Hub one-tap unsubscribe on Android; Permissions API 'change' event.
nodes.dm: Notification display with title, body, icon, actions
nodes.du: on demand, no rate limit besides OS

nodes.p: Wakes an installed site every so often to refresh data.
nodes.m: Lets an installed web app fetch updates on a schedule while closed. The browser, not the site, picks the actual times from engagement and battery.
nodes.ui: No prompt; Chrome only allows it for installed PWAs, and the permission follows engagement.
nodes.ps: Installed app only

nodes.n: Chrome and OS defenses against notification abuse
nodes.p: Browser rules that quiet, throttle and auto-revoke abusive notification sites.
nodes.m: Shows how the browser limits what an ignored or abusive site can do: a quiet prompt chip, auto-revocation, server-side throttling at FCM. A site that is ignored keeps no permission and sends nothing.
nodes.api: n/a (browser policy, Safety Hub, FCM throttling)
nodes.ui: Quiet prompt chip, Notifications blocked message in the address bar, Safety Hub revocation list, Android one-tap unsubscribe.
nodes.ps: Revoked permissions can be re-granted from Safety Hub
nodes.rv: Safety Hub, Site settings, notification Unsubscribe action

nodes.p: Lets a server wake the site in the background and show a notification.
nodes.m: Reaches the person after they leave the site. Every message must show a visible notification (userVisibleOnly), but the site learns when a device is online and which browser vendor push service it uses.
nodes.api: registration.pushManager.subscribe({userVisibleOnly: true, applicationServerKey}); push event; subscription.endpoint, getKey('p256dh'|'auth')
nodes.ui: Same notification prompt. subscribe() requires notifications permission first (Firefox and Safari also need a gesture). Safari on iOS only works for Home Screen web apps.
nodes.ps: Subscription persists until unsubscribe(), 404 or 410 from the endpoint, expiry, or clearing site data; permission revocation deletes it
nodes.rv: Site settings, unsubscribe(), pushsubscriptionchange event, 410 Gone responses
nodes.dm: Encrypted push message delivered to a service worker
nodes.du: any time while the browser runs; delivered after restart within TTL

nodes.p: A push format that shows a notification without running site code.
nodes.m: The browser renders the notification straight from JSON, so no service worker runs. Cuts battery use and removes the old silent-push abuse path; the site still learns when a device is online.
nodes.api: pushManager.subscribe via window; payload {"web_push": 8030, "notification": {title, navigate, body, lang, dir, silent, app_badge}}
nodes.ui: Same system notification prompt as classic Web Push; subscription made from the window with no service worker.
nodes.ps: Same as Web Push subscription
nodes.dm: Notification JSON handled by the browser

nodes.p: Keeps the screen on while the page is visible.
nodes.m: Stops the display from dimming or locking, which can drain battery and expose the screen. Browsers drop it when the page is hidden or battery is low, so it cannot hold the screen on in the background.
nodes.ui: No prompt in most browsers; Chrome keeps a policy gate; the permission state granted, denied or prompt follows policy and battery.
nodes.ps: Held only while the document is visible
nodes.rv: Page hidden, low battery or power saver, sentinel.release()

nodes.p: A way to keep the CPU awake while the screen is off; never shipped.
nodes.m: The spec once listed a system lock that would keep the machine awake with the screen off. No browser shipped it because of battery abuse risk. Proxies are audio playback, background sync and push.
nodes.ps: n/a

nodes.n: Push, periodic sync and background fetch
nodes.p: Ways a site can wake its service worker after the person leaves: push messages, timed sync, long downloads.
nodes.m: Push needs a notification permission; Periodic Background Sync needs an installed PWA and site engagement, with a minimum of about 12 hours between wakes; Background Fetch shows a download notice. Each lets a site run code with no tab open.
nodes.ps: Subscriptions last until the person unsubscribes, clears data, or the push service expires them
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

nodes.p: A background script registered by a site that persists after the tab is closed.
nodes.m: It can intercept every request, serve cached content, and wake for push or sync even when no page is open. The browser stops it after about 30 seconds idle, but the registration stays until cleared. Safari deletes it after 7 days of non use.
nodes.ps: Registration persists with no fixed expiry. Script checked for update at most every 24 hours. Idle stop after about 30 s (Chrome)
nodes.rv: Clear site data, browser privacy settings
